name: Sucellus

attributes.attribute: a Continental Celtic god who carries a hammer
sometimes set beside the woodland god Silvanus
alone could stand for the god
read as a fertility god of the sun and the wildwood

sources: Green, Miranda. Symbol and Image in Celtic Religious Art. London: Routledge, 1989, 46, 75.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Sucellus is a Continental Celtic god. The name is read as the striker, and in his arms he carries the sign of that name, a great hammer or mallet. The same tool is the weapon of the Irish Dagda. The god appears across Gaul, and the Romans did not give him the name of one of their own gods, though they now and then set him beside their woodland god Silvanus. The sculptors show him as a full-grown, bearded man with a fine head of curly hair. The look is kind, turned on the viewer. He wears native dress, a tunic and a cloak, not the Roman or Greek garb. His hammer was so much his sign that the hammer alone could stand for the god. It is not linked to the thunder of Zeus or Odin in the usual way. The hammer was read as the power that drives green life up from the earth. So Sucellus is a god of the wild and of the returning growth, and for that gift he was also a god of healing.
